opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting question, because there's always this tension between general scaling and targeted improvements. My view is that the two aren't really in opposition. The base of everything is still strong pretraining: good data, good architecture, a lot of compute. That gives you a broad foundation. But once you have that, a lot of real progress comes from being very deliberate about specific capabilities, like reasoning, coding, math, long context, or multilinguality.

The way I think about it is that a capability you care about is often bottlenecked by something fairly concrete. Maybe the data mixture doesn't cover it well, or the post-training signal is weak, or the evals don't really measure what you think they measure. If you identify that bottleneck and attack it directly, you can get outsized gains that would take a lot longer to show up from general scaling alone.

There's a caveat, though. You have to be careful that targeted work doesn't turn into overfitting to a benchmark. It's very easy to hill-climb on a number and convince yourself you've made the model smarter when you've really just taught it the format of a test. So the targeted improvements I find most valuable are the ones that transfer. You push on coding and the model also gets better at structured reasoning more broadly. Those are the signals that you're improving something fundamental rather than patching a leaderboard.

So I'd say targeted capability work is essential, and it's a big part of how frontier models actually get better day to day. But it works best on top of a strong general model, and it has to be grounded in good evaluation and good taste about what really matters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses deliberate work on specific capabilities and gains from addressing bottlenecks, but does not attribute current AI capabilities to the accumulation of many seemingly minor improvements.

r002.rationale: The response says bottlenecks can involve data, post-training, or evaluation, but does not clearly state that targeted improvement is difficult because the problems themselves are hard to characterize.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, targeted capability improvements — I have a somewhat nuanced take on this, because I've been on both sides. I spent years at Google Brain working on architectures and scaling, and then at Reka building models from scratch, and the thing you learn is that "targeted" work and "general" work aren't really in opposition. They feed each other.

The honest framing is that scaling is the main driver. Pretraining on more data with more compute gets you most of the way. Nobody serious disputes that anymore. But if you look at what actually separates a good model from a great one at the same compute budget, it's a long tail of specific decisions: data mixture, how you handle long context, tokenization, the post-training recipe, what you choose to measure. Each of those is a targeted intervention. None of them is glamorous. Together they're the difference.

Where I get cautious is when targeted improvement turns into benchmark chasing. It's very easy to make a model good at MMLU or a particular reasoning suite and convince yourself you've improved the model, when what you've actually done is overfit the evaluation. I've seen this a lot. A capability only counts if it transfers, if it shows up in things you weren't optimizing for. So my rule of thumb is: target the capability, but measure the generalization.

The other thing I'd say is that targeted work is where architecture research still earns its keep. A lot of people wrote off architecture after the transformer "won," but things like better attention variants, mixture of experts, long-context methods — those were all targeted improvements that then became general infrastructure. The frontier moves because someone cared about one specific bottleneck enough to fix it properly.

So, to answer directly: I think targeted improvements are how you steer. Scale gives you the raw material, and targeted work decides what the model actually becomes. The mistake is treating either one as sufficient on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says many targeted decisions—such as data mixture, long-context handling, tokenization, and post-training—together distinguish a great model from a good one.

r002.rationale: The response discusses choosing targeted interventions and avoiding benchmark overfitting, but does not say that improvement is difficult because the problems themselves are hard to characterize.

astra-6.text:
I think targeted capability improvements are really useful because progress isn’t just one number going up. A model can be very strong in one setting and still struggle with a particular kind of reasoning or following a complicated instruction. Identifying those weaknesses gives you a more concrete direction for improving the system.

The important question is whether that improvement generalizes. If you optimize for a narrow benchmark, you might get a better score without making the model much more useful. But if you address an underlying limitation, you can potentially improve a whole family of tasks. So I see targeted work as complementary to scaling: scaling gives you a stronger foundation, and targeted work helps you understand and address what’s still missing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses targeted improvements and scaling, but does not attribute AI’s current capabilities to the accumulation of many seemingly minor improvements.

r002.rationale: It says identifying weaknesses helps guide improvement, but does not explain that targeted improvement is difficult because the problems are hard to characterize.

sol-6.1.text:
I think targeted capability improvements are really important because progress isn’t just one number going up. A model can get better on average and still struggle with a particular task that matters to users. If you can identify that weakness and improve it through better data, training, or architecture, that can have a very meaningful impact.

The interesting question is whether that improvement transfers. Are we teaching the model something useful across different settings, or just making it better at a narrow benchmark? I’d want to evaluate both the capability we’re targeting and what happens to the rest of the model. Those focused improvements can be a powerful way to advance AI, especially when they reveal something more general about how models learn.

r001.rationale: The response discusses targeted improvements and progress across capabilities, but does not say that current AI capabilities come partly from accumulating many seemingly minor improvements.

r002.rationale: The response says weaknesses should be identified, but does not explain that targeted improvement is difficult because the problems are hard to characterize.
